paragraphs: Kol dam behema vechayya veop veken dam shelil, asur min hattora; abal dam dagim vachagabim muttar min hattora, veaseru chaza"l mishshum marit haayin; veim yesh bo hekker qasqassim, muttar. veken dam haadam muttar min hattora; vaasaruhu chaza"l im peresh, mishshum marit haayin. lepikak im nashak hakkikkar beshinnayv veyatza dam venitlaklek hakkikkar, tzarik legarero kede sheyyokal hakkikkar, abal dam sheodennu ben hashshinnayim, motzetzo veeno choshesh. veken hu haddin im etzbao metaptep dam mimmenna, yukal lehannicha etzbao bepiv im haddam metaptep lehedya, shennikkar shehu metaptep meetzbao; abal im nipsaq hattiptup venishar haetzba meluklak bedam, asur lehannicha bepiv mishshum marit haayin.

clarification.explanation: Blood of a domestic animal, wild animal, fowl, or a fetus is Torah-forbidden. Blood of fish and locusts is Torah-permitted, but the Sages forbade it out of concern for appearance, and if it has a distinguishing mark of scales (making it recognizable as fish blood) it is permitted. Human blood is Torah-permitted, and the Sages forbade it once it has "emerged" (left the body) out of concern for appearance. Therefore if a person bit into a loaf with his teeth and blood emerged, staining the loaf, one must scrape off the blood in order to eat it; but blood still between the teeth may be sucked without concern. Likewise, if a person's finger is dripping blood, he may put it in his mouth as long as the blood is actually dripping (so it is recognizable as coming from his finger); but if the dripping has stopped and the finger remains stained with blood, it is forbidden to put it in his mouth, out of concern for appearance.
takeaways: Blood of a domestic/wild animal or fowl is Torah-forbidden; blood of fish and of humans is Torah-permitted but rabbinically forbidden.
Blood between the teeth or actively dripping from a finger is permitted; blood that has emerged and clotted is forbidden.

paragraphs: Bibhema vechayya veop dam hannepesh bekaret, abal dam haebarim belo-taaseh; vehaynu im yotze lachutz o nitzrar beebar o shennitorer latzet venibla bemaqom acher, abal im haddam odennu babbasar velo peresh velo nitzrar sham, hare zeh muttar; lepikak muttar leekol basar chay, ubilbad sheyyedichennu min dam shemmeluklak bo, ubilbad shello yihyeh beoto basar chutin sheyyesh bahem dam.

clarification.explanation: In a domestic animal, wild animal, and fowl: the "blood of life" (flowing at the time of slaughter) carries the penalty of karet, but the blood of the limbs carries only a negative prohibition — that is, if it emerged outward, pooled in a limb, or was stirred to emerge and was absorbed elsewhere. But blood still within the flesh that has not emerged or pooled there is permitted. Therefore it is permitted to eat raw meat, provided one rinses off the blood staining it and it contains no veins with blood in them.
takeaways: The blood of life carries karet; the blood of the limbs carries a negative prohibition (if it emerged or pooled).
Raw meat is permitted if rinsed of blood and free of blood-containing veins.

paragraphs: Nitzrar haddam babbasar mechamat makka, tzarik lechateko kamma qeraim, umolecho kedino umibbeshello. veim rotzeh litzloto, muttar belo chittuk umelicha, denura mashab shaab haddam.

clarification.explanation: If blood pooled in the flesh due to a wound, the area must be cut with several incisions, salted according to the law, and cooked. But if one wishes to roast it, this is permitted without cutting or salting, since the fire draws out and expels the blood.
takeaways: Blood pooled from a wound: the area is cut, salted, and cooked.
For roasting, it is permitted without cutting or salting, since the fire draws out the blood.

paragraphs: Yesh kamma chutin bebasar sheyyesh bahem dam shetztzarik lechattekan; upoh irenu bagdad y", hagam shennohagin lehotzi kol hachutin ap becheleq panim shel habbehema, apillu hake nohagim leshabber kol haatzamot veen mannichin etzem shalem. gam poh irenu bagdad nohagin lachtok rosh hakkanap beop qodem melicha, kede shedderek sham yotze haddam al-yede melicha.

clarification.explanation: There are several blood-containing veins in the meat that must be cut out. In Baghdad, although it is customary to remove all the veins even from the animal's internal parts, it is also customary to break all the bones, leaving no bone whole. Likewise in Baghdad it is customary to cut off the tip of the wing in a fowl before salting, so the blood can exit through there during salting.
takeaways: The blood-bearing veins are removed, and all bones are broken (Baghdad custom).
The wing tip of a fowl is cut off before salting so the blood can exit through it.

paragraphs: Nimtza tippat dam bebetza, ben bechelmon, ben bechelbon - nahagu shelemim veken rabbim leesor; v"g demaran za"l lo asar ella bechelmon, abal bechelbon pasaq, zoreq haddam veokel hashshear - rauy leesor bekol gavna, veken nohagim poh irenu bagdad. vegam bebetza bat yoma im nimtza dam asura, dela pelug rabbanan. veheka denimtza dam bebetza shebbime hattarnegolet, yesh omerim dezoreq haddam veokel hashshear, umihu nakon lehachmir bah kedin betza bat yoma; veayyen machaziq beraka, seip qatan yo"d. veda d"p sheamarnu leesor habbetza shennimtza bah dam, ben bechelmon, ben bechelbon, kemo shekkatab mvr"m za"l behaggahat hashshulchan, mikkol maqom bishat haddechaq o behepsed merubbeh yesh lismok al hammattirim benimtza bechelbon chutz laqqesher velo nitpashshet kelal; veayyen "erek-hashshulchan". vehinneh inyan haqqesher hu yadua, sheyyesh lechelbon qesher berosho hachad, vehu dabar shennitpas mizzera hazzakar nikkar laayin, shennireh shehu mequshshar yoter mishshear chelbon, vehu dabar muat qashur kemo chutin; vegam bechelmon yesh gam ken qesher, vehu bidmut keter agol kimlo rochab adasha gedola; uledaat haggeonim, yetzirat haeprocha min hachelmon, velaken machmirim bechelmon tepe, veken sebarat mera"n za"l; ak haroe"h veroqeach sebira lehu, yetzirat haeprocha min hachelbon, lekak machmirin bechelbon tepe, vela qayma lan kevatayhu.

clarification.explanation: A drop of blood found in an egg, whether in the yolk (the yellow) or the white (the albumen), was customarily forbidden for the entire egg, and although Maran forbade it only in the yolk, it is proper to forbid it in either case, and this is the Baghdad custom. Even in a fresh egg (from the day it was laid), if blood is found, it is forbidden. And in an egg still inside the hen, some say one discards the blood and eats the rest, but nevertheless it is proper to be stringent with it as with a fresh egg. Nevertheless, in a pressing situation or great loss, one may rely on the lenient authorities when the blood is found in the white outside the "knot" and has not spread. The "knot" is the place where the male's seed was received (appearing as threads at the pointed end of the white), and in the yolk the knot is like a round crown shape. According to the Geonim (and Maran), the chick forms from the yolk, and therefore they are stricter regarding it; but the Ra'ah and the Rokeach hold the opposite, that the chick forms from the white, and are therefore stricter regarding the white — though the halacha does not follow them, and the halacha follows the Geonim and Maran, who are stricter regarding the yolk.
takeaways: Blood in an egg, whether in the yolk or white, forbids the whole egg (the Baghdad and stricter custom).
In a case of great loss, one may be lenient with blood in the white outside the knot that has not spread.
The Ra'ah and Rokeach disagree, holding the chick forms from the white and therefore being stricter regarding it, but the halacha does not follow them.

paragraphs: Hannotenim betzim al kissuy haqqedera kede lehitztammeq venimtza dam beachat mehem, muttar hachammin shebbaqqedera, veeno neesar mikkoach habbetzim.

clarification.explanation: One who places eggs on top of a pot's lid so they cook down from its heat, and blood is found in one of them — the hot food in the pot is permitted and is not forbidden on account of the egg.
takeaways: Blood found in an egg placed atop a pot's lid — the food in the pot remains permitted.

paragraphs: Betzim muzarot shennipsedu mechamat shehattarnegolet yasheba alehem - im en haadam nimna leakelam mishshum istenisot, hare hem muttarim, ubilbad sheyyizroq haddam; vedavqa beyadua desapena meara. upoh irenu bagdad nohagim shello leekol betzim muzarot; chada, mishshum meisot, veyesh bahem mishshum sheyyaqotz; veod, en yadua lanu ezeh hi sipna meara, veal harob hem mizzakar; veod, gam beyadua desapena meara demattir mera"n za"l apillu yasheba alehem yamim harbeh - ha yesh machmirim im yasheba alehem shelosha yamim meet leet, ubekol achat yesh lachush shemma yasheba g' yamim, lekak en okelim betzim muzarot kelal; veayyen bemachaziq beraka vechakemat adam.

clarification.explanation: Addled eggs spoiled from the hen sitting on them — if a person is not deterred from eating them due to squeamishness, they are permitted, provided the blood is discarded, and specifically when it is known they are "formed from the ground" (created spontaneously, without a male). But in Baghdad it was customary not to eat addled eggs at all: due to repulsiveness and disgust; because it is not known which are "formed from the ground" and most come from a male; and because some are stringent if the hen sat on it for three full days, and with each one there is concern it may have sat for three days.
takeaways: Addled eggs are permitted only if "formed from the ground" and the blood is discarded.
In Baghdad they are not eaten at all, due to repulsiveness and uncertainty.

paragraphs: Muttar ligmoa betza tzeluya, veen tzarik lehashgicha im yesh bah dam o lav, veken haya noheg rabbenu haari"y za"l, deeno choshesh libdoq, desamekinan al rob betzim sheen bahem dam; umikkol maqom kesheosin maakol im betzim bemachabat, nohagim lirot uleayyen bebetzim beet shemmeshabberim otam im yesh bahem dam o lav; veayyen bemachaziq beraka, seip qatan t', yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted to gulp down a roasted egg without needing to check it for blood, and so was the Arizal's practice, relying on the fact that most eggs contain no blood. Nevertheless, when preparing a dish from eggs in a pan, it is customary to examine them for blood when cracking them open.
takeaways: A roasted egg may be gulped down without examination, since most eggs lack blood.
When cracking eggs for a cooked dish, it is customary to examine them.

paragraphs: Bene-adam sheqqonim basar umannichin oto bequppot sheddarkam lehannicha bahem perot viraqot vekikkarot lechem vekayyotze, tzarik limchot bahem shello yaasu ken, mippene shehaddam sheal habbasar nidbaq baqquppot, veaach"k nidbaq beperot viraqot vekikkarot; vaapillu im yirtzu lahadicham, la arik lemebad haki, kevan dehave midi delav orecheh bahadacha, ukemo shekkatub besiman tz"; veayyen peri chadash, siman s"t, seip qatan k"d, vehebio hammachaziq beraka, siman s"v, seip qatan y"g, ayyen sham. vaapillu im habbasar nimlach, gam ken en lehannicho baqquppot hahem, dechayeshinan dilma okel otam bechalab, ukemo shekkatab besipte daat za"l.

clarification.explanation: Those who buy meat and place it in baskets normally used for fruit, vegetables, and loaves of bread must be protested against, since the blood on the meat sticks to the baskets and afterward to the fruit and bread. And even if one wishes to rinse them, this does not help, since fruit and bread cannot be cleaned by rinsing. And even if the meat is already salted, it should not be placed in these baskets, out of concern one might eat the fruit together with dairy.
takeaways: Meat should not be placed in baskets used for fruit and bread, since blood sticks to them.
This applies even to salted meat, out of concern for eating the fruit with dairy afterward.

paragraphs: Habbasar im bishshelo belo melicha, neesar, mippene shehaddam yiprosh "y habbishshul, vechozer venibla betoko, lepikak tzarik lemalecho techilla kede lebashshelo; mihu, tzarik lehaddicha habbasar qodem melicha min haddam shealayv beayin, veaach"k yimlachennu. ulekattechilla tzarik lishroto bemayim chatzi shaa qodem melicha, veyaddichennu vishapshepennu yapeh yapeh, vekol maqom sheyyeraeh bo dam tzarik shipshup yoter yapeh; ubediabad im lo asa sheriyya bemayim, ella raq hiddicho hadacha mealleya, mehanne leh. veyesh meqomot sheen nohagim lishrot habbasar, ella maddichim oto hadacha mealleya umolechim oto kistam mera"n za"l shello zakar sheriyya, ella hadacha bilbad; veken nohagim poh irenu bagdad y"; umikkol maqom tzerikim lehizzaher lehaddicha heteb uleshapshep beyadayim bekoach, ki hashshipshup hu haiqqar. veyishpok hammayim shehedicha veshipshep bahem, veyachazor veyadicha paam shenit bemayim shenit, veyishpok hammayim veyadicha paam shelishit, ad sheyyihyu hammayim beli shum mareh roshem dam kelal; umissetama beshalosh peamim yihyu hammayim neqiyyim beli shum mareh roshem dam kelal; veayyen sha"k vechavvot daat vechakemat adam ushear acharonim za"l.

clarification.explanation: Meat cooked without salting is forbidden, since the blood is released during cooking and is reabsorbed into the meat, and therefore it must first be salted. And before salting, one must rinse off the visible blood on it, and as the primary practice soak it in water for half an hour, then rinse and scrub it well (and where blood is visible, more scrubbing). After the fact, if it was not soaked but only rinsed well, this suffices. In some places they do not soak but only rinse and salt (following Maran's plain wording mentioning only rinsing), and so in Baghdad; nevertheless one must rinse well and scrub forcefully with the hands, since the scrubbing is the essential part. One should pour out the rinse water and rinse again up to three times, until the water shows no trace of blood at all.
takeaways: Meat is salted before cooking, and rinsed and soaked (as the primary practice) before salting.
Forceful scrubbing is essential; one rinses until the water is free of any trace of blood.

paragraphs: Lipamim yimmatze etzel mokere habbasar basar shello nimkar babboqer venishar ad haereb o ad yom sheni; vezeh, haddam shealayv nityabbesh veniqrash, veeno yotze bahadacha bilbad; al-ken apillu poh irenu shennahagu bahadacha bilbad, mikkol maqom basar zeh tzerikin lishroto bemayim chatzi shaa, veaach"k yedicho oto heteb vishapshepu bekoach, ubiprat meqom bet hashshechita, veaach"k yimlachennu.

clarification.explanation: Sometimes meat remains unsold with butchers in the morning and stays until evening or the next day, and the blood on it has dried and clotted and does not come out by rinsing alone. Therefore even in Baghdad, where the custom is to rinse only, such meat must be soaked in water for half an hour, then rinsed well and scrubbed forcefully, especially at the site of slaughter, and then salted.
takeaways: Old meat with dried blood requires half an hour of soaking even where the custom is otherwise to rinse only.
One scrubs forcefully, especially at the slaughter site, and then salts.

paragraphs: Im achar shehedicha chatak kol netach lishtayim o leshalosh chatikot, tzarik lachazor lehaddicha; veim achar shechatak melach velo hedicha paam achat, yesh lehattir behepsed merubbeh, abal belo hepsed merubbeh tzarik lachush. veim malach habbasar veshaha shiur melicha veaach"k chatak, en tzarik lachazor lehaddicha velimloach shenit, shehare palat kol damo; veayyen chakemat adam.

clarification.explanation: If, after rinsing the meat, each cut was divided into two or three pieces, one must rinse again (the cut surface). And if one salted after cutting without rinsing again, this may be permitted in a case of great loss, but without great loss one should be concerned. And if the meat was salted and left for the required salting time and only then cut, there is no need to rinse and salt again, since it has already released all its blood.
takeaways: Cutting after rinsing requires re-rinsing the cut surface before salting.
Cutting after the meat has already been salted for the required time requires no repetition.

paragraphs: Achar shehedicha habbasar yamtin ad sheyyittaptepu hammayim qodem sheyyimlachennu, kede shello yimmas hammelach mechamat ribbuy hammayim sheodennu al habbasar velo yotzi dam, abal lo yamtin ad sheyyitnaggeb legamre, deaz lo yimmas hammelach kelal, veyishshaer yabesh velo yaaseh peullato lehotzi haddam.

clarification.explanation: After rinsing the meat, one should wait until the water drips off before salting it, so the salt does not dissolve from the excess water on the meat and fail to draw out blood. But one should not wait until it is entirely dry, since then the salt would not dissolve at all, remaining dry and failing to draw out the blood.
takeaways: One waits for the water to drip off before salting, so the salt does not dissolve.
But not until fully dry, or the salt will not work at all.

paragraphs: Im malach velo hedicha techilla, apillu im lo nimlach ella raq meat kederek shemmolechin letzali, vaapillu lo shaha bemilcho shiur melicha, hare zeh asur; mihu, behepsed merubbeh o beereb-shabbat vei epshar lehakin acher, az yesh lo taqqana sheyyedichennu veyimlachennu shenit; veayyen machaziq beraka, siman s"t, ot d' ushear acharonim za"l. veim lo hedicha umalach shenit ubishshelo, en lo taqqana veasur, vaapillu behepsed merubbeh usheat haddechaq, ukemo shekkatab happeri chadash ukereti upeleti umachaziq beraka, veayyen sipte daat, seip qatan y"b.

clarification.explanation: If one salted without first rinsing, even if only a little salt was used as for roasting, and even if it was not left for the required salting time, this is forbidden. In a case of great loss, or on Sabbath eve when nothing else can be prepared, there is a remedy: rinsing and salting it again. But if it was neither rinsed nor re-salted, but simply cooked as is, there is no remedy and it is forbidden, even in a case of great loss and a pressing situation.
takeaways: Salting without first rinsing is forbidden; in great loss, one may rinse and re-salt.
Cooking without any rinsing or re-salting is entirely forbidden, even in great loss.

paragraphs: Chatika shennimlecha velo huddecha hadacha harishona, venitareba baacherot shehuddechu kedinan venimlechu, veen makkirin otah chatika - "g demin haddin betela berob, mikkol maqom tzarik sheyyachazor vidichem veyimlachem shenit, meachar dela nitbashshela adayin, ukemo shekkatab mahari"y lebet-levi, siman l"; veayyen kinnat haggedola, haggahat habbet yosep, ot tz"h, mah shekkatab al hassapeq sapeqa sheasa harab bazeh, ayyen sham; ubeemet qayma lan deabedinan sepeq sepeqa biplugta derabbevata.

clarification.explanation: A piece of meat salted without having been rinsed first (the initial rinsing), which became mixed with pieces properly rinsed and salted, and cannot be identified — even though by strict law it is nullified in the majority, nevertheless all the pieces must be rinsed and salted again, since they have not yet been cooked.
takeaways: An unrinsed piece mixed in — even though nullified in the majority, all pieces must be rinsed and salted again, since they have not yet been cooked.

paragraphs: Lo yimlach bemelach daq keqemach, sheeno maplit yapeh; veim en lo melach acher ella raq zeh haddaq, muttar limloach bo. veim malach bo veaach"k hebiu lo melach acher shehu benoni, en matrichin oto lemalecho bazeh paam shenit, dehave bediabad, vekannizkar besipte daat, seip qatan y"z. velo yimlach bemelach gas beyoter shennopel hammelach bazeh meal habbasar elak veelak, ella yishchaqennu techilla sheyyihyeh benoni, veyimlach bo.

clarification.explanation: One should not salt with salt as fine as flour, since it does not draw out the blood well; but if one has only this fine salt, it is permitted to salt with it. And if one salted with it and afterward medium salt was brought, one is not required to salt again, since this is after the fact. Likewise one should not salt with salt too coarse, which falls off the sides of the meat, but should first grind it to a medium consistency and salt with that.
takeaways: Salt should be medium — neither as fine as flour nor too coarse.
In a pinch, fine salt is permitted, and one need not re-salt afterward.

paragraphs: Shiur shehiyyat habbasar bemelach tzarik shaa achat, dehaynu shishshim daqqim; ubediabad saggi beshiur mil. veameru siman al zeh: "bemelach timlach" (vayyiqra yb, yg)- misseper "bemelach" oleh mispar "mil". od ameru siman acher: "lebilti akol haddam" (debarim yb, kg)- sope tebot "mil". ubishat haddechaq shetztzarik lemaher likbod orechin o likbod shabbat, sheen lo shehut lehamtin shaa achat, o shehu yotze ladderek veen mamtinim alayv, o letzorek choleh shetztzarik leekol bimhera, yesh lehattir bekol hane beshiur mil gam lekattechilla. veha deamerinan muttar lekattechilla bemil likbod orechin, haynu davqa beorechin shehem baale tora ubaale shem tob umaasim tobim, o ani ben-tobim, o ashirim sheenam baale risha sherauy lekabbedam, vekannizkar b"pitche-teshuba", seip qatan y"b. umi shezzimmen et chabero lisod etzlo, have biklal orechim; veim hu yodea shetztzarik lehaqel bishbilo beinyan zeh, lo yezammenu; veraq im kebar zemanno vehutzrak lemaher – shari, degadol kebod habberiyyot vekannizkar sham.

clarification.explanation: The required time for meat to remain in salt is one hour (sixty minutes), and after the fact, the time it takes to walk a "mil" (a Talmudic distance unit) suffices. Mnemonic hints for this: the numerical value of "bamelach" (in salt) equals that of "mil," and the final letters of "lest you eat the blood" spell "mil." In a pressing situation requiring haste — for the honor of guests, for the honor of the Sabbath, for a traveler departing, or for the need of a patient — it is permitted to rely on the measure of a mil even as the primary practice. And the leniency for the honor of guests applies specifically to guests who are Torah scholars of good reputation, or a poor person of good family, or respectable wealthy people. And one who invites his friend to a meal is included among "guests"; but if he knows in advance he will need to be lenient for his sake, he should not invite him — only if he has already invited him and then needed to hurry is it permitted, since the honor of people is of great importance.
takeaways: The required salting time is one hour; after the fact and in a pressing situation (guests, the Sabbath, travel, illness), the time of a mil suffices.
The leniency for guests applies to respectable guests; if already invited and haste becomes necessary, it is permitted due to the importance of human dignity.

paragraphs: Achar shemmalach habbasar veshaha shiur melicha karauy, lo yebashshelo ella "y hadacha shettihyeh beopen zeh vehu techillat hakkol yenappetz hammelach shealayv o yishtepennu bemayim kesheochazo beyado baavir veaach"k yasim mayim harbeh betok hakkeli sherotzeh lahadicho bo kede sheyyitbattel koach hammelach shebbatztzir beribbuy hammayim sheqqadam lehannicho betok hakkeli veachar shehinnicha hammayim bakkeli yannicha bo habbasar veyaddichennu shelosha peamim uben hadacha lahadacha yannicha habbasar bikli acher menuqqab ad sheyyishtop hakkeli shemmedicha habbasar betoko im yirtzeh lehannicha betok hakkeli hamnuqqab shemmalu bo tzarik sheyyirchatz techilla et hakkeli hamnuqqab hahe min tzir hammelicha sheyyesh bo veim lo nappetz hammelach shealayv velo shetapo en leesor ki hammayim harabbim shemmannicha bakkeli lahadicho bahem mebattelim koach hammelach vaapillu im yihyu muatim im kol zeh mebattelim koach hatztzir.

clarification.explanation: After salting and leaving it for the required time, before cooking one must rinse as follows: first shake off the salt on the meat or wipe it off in the air, then put plenty of water in the vessel to be used for rinsing (enough to nullify the strength of the salt and the brine), then place the meat in it and rinse it three times. Between rinsings, place the meat in a different perforated vessel until the rinsing vessel is washed; and if one wishes to place it back in the perforated vessel used for salting, one should first wash off the brine from it. And if one did not shake off the salt or rinse it off first, there is no reason to forbid it, since the plentiful water in the vessel nullifies the strength of the salt and brine, and even a small amount of water nullifies the strength of the brine.
takeaways: The final rinsing: shake off the salt, and rinse in plenty of water three times.
The plentiful water nullifies the strength of the salt and brine, even if the salt was not shaken off first.

paragraphs: Ishah shebbishshelah basar veshakecha im malecha oto o lav yesh leesor missapeq veyesh mattirim behepsed merubbeh veayyen bemachaziq beraka seip qatan y"d umihu im zokeret shemmelachah oto ella shakecha im melachtu meshanne tzedadin o raq mitztzad echad hare zeh muttar gam behepsed muat veayyen peri toar seip qatan y"d.

clarification.explanation: A woman who cooked meat and forgot whether she salted it should be forbidden out of doubt, though some permit it in a case of great loss. But if she remembers salting it, only forgetting whether she salted both sides or just one, this is permitted even in a case of minor loss.
takeaways: Forgetting entirely whether it was salted — forbidden out of doubt (some permit in great loss).
Remembering it was salted, but unsure if on both sides — permitted even in minor loss.

paragraphs: Basar shennimlach venitbashshel belo hadacha acharona, apillu ledidan dela qayma lan chatika naaset nebela bishar issurin, ella raq bebasar bechalab - tzarik sheyyihyeh shishshim keneged hammelach shebbo, vegam baenan shishshim keneged dam peleta sheal pene habbasar; vekol mah sheyyesh baqqedera mitztarep lashshishshim, abal gup haqqedera atzmah eno mitztarep. veim yesh baqqedera kol kak kemo shiur hachatika shennimlecha velo huddecha, hakkol shari, devadday ikka shishshim keneged hammelach sheal hachatika, yaan dehachatika atzmah vadday hi sheloshim neged hammelach shealeha; veim en shishshim baqqedera neged hammelach vedam peleta sheal habbasar, apillu lo husam ella bikli sheni shehayyad soledet bo, hakkol asur; veyesh meqillin behepsed merubbeh bikli sheni shehayyad soledet bo, abal im en hayyad soledet bo, muttar apillu behepsed muat. vbsh"q "rab-pealim" heeleti bs"d, deshiur zeh shekkatab mvr"m, dehachatika atzmah hi erek sheloshim keneged hammelach, en zeh gezerat chakamim, ella taluy haddabar lepi reot ene hammoreh; debeemet en kol hachatikot shavot bazeh, veen hammelach hannishar al gabbe habbasar achar shiur melicha hu shaveh; vesham hebeti dibre "berit-melach", dap m"z, demashma middebarayv - ha debaenan shishshim keneged hammelach, haynu im hu beayin, abal im namas kol hammelach, en tzarik leshaer ella keneged hallachluchit hannimtza al habbasar; vediyyeq lah middibre hattur umera"n za"l; veayyen chavvat daat bechiddushim, seip qatan l"g, yeuyyan sham. veod hebeti sham dibre haggaon hechasid "kanpe-yona", sheheela vezeh leshono: delipamim yesh shishshim bachatika im hi aba, velaken im nireh lehammoreh sheyyesh shishshim bachatika neged milcho umah shennidbaq bo, yukal leshaer lehakshiro kak beli sapeq, veken mashmaut hashshulchan aruk; ad kan leshono harab za"l, yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: Meat that was salted and cooked without a final rinsing must have sixty times the volume in the pot relative to the salt on it and the blood-release on the meat's surface. Everything in the pot counts toward the sixty, but the body of the pot itself does not count. If there is in the pot a volume equal to the unrinsed piece, everything is permitted, since the piece itself counts as roughly thirty relative to its own salt. And if there is not sixty in the pot, even if it was placed only in a second vessel still hot enough that "a hand recoils from it," everything is forbidden (though some are lenient in a case of great loss for a second vessel); and if it is not hot enough that a hand recoils, it is permitted even in a case of minor loss. And our teacher wrote that this measure (that the piece counts as roughly thirty relative to its salt) is not a fixed decree but depends on the judgment of the halachic authority, since not all pieces are equal; and some say that if all the salt dissolved, one need only measure against the moisture on the meat; and if it appears to the authority that there is sixty within the piece itself (when it is thick), he may permit it.
takeaways: Meat salted and cooked without a final rinse requires sixty times the volume against the salt and blood-release.
The measure depends on the authority's judgment; a thick piece may itself contain the required sixty.

paragraphs: Hammelach shemmalach bo paam achat – asur limloach bo paam acheret; ubediabad im malach bo paam acheret: im kebar nitbashshel habbasar, muttar; veim adayin lo nitbashshel, yedichennu veyachazor veyimlachennu, ak yizzaher lemalecho lebaddo, velo im basar acher shetztzarik limlicha; veayyen b"sipte-daat", seip-qatan m, yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: Salt already used once for salting may not be used to salt again. After the fact, if it was used again: if the meat has already been cooked, it is permitted; if not yet cooked, one should rinse it and salt it again, being careful to salt it alone and not together with other meat that still requires salting.
takeaways: Salt already used for salting may not be reused.
After the fact: if cooked, permitted; if not, rinse and re-salt alone.

paragraphs: En melicha moelet lebasar liplot damo ella raq bemelach; umah shekkatab b"halakot qetannot", siman ry"ch, beinyan sukkar - haynu leinyan qarebban, abal en kavvanato lomar sheyyimlach bo habbasar lehaplit dam. veayyen "imre-esh", yoreh dea, siman k"ch, mah sheqqara tiggar al chakam shehora limloach b"haalyon" shenniqra bilshon chakamim "tzerip", vekatab sheen libdot dabar millibbenu, veen lanu ella mah sheamera tora: "bemelach timlach" (vayyiqra b, yg); veken katab "shoel umeshib" qamma, siman qm"b; veken katab haggaon "ketab-soper", yoreh dea, siman l"z, shehammoreh - shoteh vegas rucha, ayyen sham; veken katab "dibre-chayyim", yo"d, siman k"h. veayyen lehaggaon "yad-eliezer", siman "d, yeuyyan sham. veim katebu ken bazeh ha"tzerip" shehu charip, kol shekken besukkar; al-ken en limloach beshum dabar chutz min hammelach. umah shekkatab beiqqere-hd"t, siman yu"d, ot l"v, limloach besukkar - achar harob taut hu, vaapillu besukkar shel meqomo. veayyen leharab haggaon rabbi chayyim palagi'y za"l b"rucha-chayyim", siman t', ot Adonai, shehittir besukkar; veshub hora harab za"l velo bosh, ki taut hu zeh, vehebi dibre harab "chesed leabraham" teomim, siman l"b, shessatam happetach bishar minim chutz min hammelach, vaapillu bediabad oser gam et hakkelim, yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: Salting is effective in drawing blood out of meat only with salt itself. What is mentioned regarding sugar concerns the sacrificial offering, not the drawing out of blood. Several of the great halachic authorities spoke out sharply against anyone who ruled to salt with "tzarif" (a caustic substance) or with sugar, since one may not invent anything from one's own mind, and we have only what the Torah said, "with salt shall it be salted" — and they even forbade the vessels after the fact. And if they were this stringent regarding the caustic tzarif, all the more so regarding sugar. Even Rabbi Chaim Palagi, who initially permitted sugar, retracted and ruled it was an error. Therefore one should not salt with anything other than salt.
takeaways: Blood is drawn out only with actual salt, not sugar or other substances.
The great authorities forbade this sharply, even forbidding the vessels after the fact.

paragraphs: Basar shennitbashshel belo melicha, o shennimlach velo shaha shiur melicha venitbashshel, vaapillu shello nitbashshel legamre ella raq samu oto biqdera shehayyad soledet bo - tzarik sheyyihyeh battabshil shebbaqqedera shishshim keneged oto basar, veaz muttar gam oto basar atzmo shello nimlach; veim en shishshim, hakkol asur vegam haqqedera asura. vehu haddin hashshumman shennitbashshel belo melicha, detzarik name shishshim neged kol hashshumman. veim nishpak hattabshil vesapeq im haya bo shishshim, yesh leesor. veayyen "bet-hillel" v"erek-hashshulchan". veim hayu hammayim shebbaqqedera rotechin meod keshennatenu sham et habbasar shello nimlach, ubarur lahem haddabar hazzeh, yesh lehaqel bishat haddechaq, kegon shehu ereb-shabbat, o heka deikka hepsed merubbeh, mishshum dehave chalita, shennityabbesh damo betoko veeno polet; veayyen "erek-hashshulchan" veaqeri-hd"t v"shiyyure-beraka".

clarification.explanation: Meat cooked without salting, or salted without being left for the required salting time and then cooked, and even meat merely placed in a pot hot enough that "a hand recoils from it," requires sixty times the volume of the dish relative to that meat, and then even the meat itself is permitted; if there is not sixty, everything is forbidden, including the pot. Likewise, fat cooked without salting requires sixty against it. And if the dish spilled and there is doubt whether it contained sixty, one should forbid it. But if the water in the pot was very boiling hot at the time the meat was placed in it, and this is clearly known, one may be lenient in a pressing situation (Sabbath eve or great loss), since this is "scalding," whereby the blood dries inside and is not released.
takeaways: Meat cooked without salting requires sixty times its volume, or everything is forbidden, including the pot.
Very boiling water at the time of placing the meat in ("scalding") allows leniency in a pressing situation, since the blood does not release.
